Quick quiz for Texas employers: is a 15-minute break paid?

Yes. Under federal law, rest breaks of about 20 minutes or less count as hours worked.

Texas itself sets no break rules for adults. So the length of every break is your call, and every minute of it matters.

If the nearest food is a drive away, a 15-minute break goes to traffic. Food in the building gives that time back.

What does your site do for breaks? Tell us below.

Full guide at the link in bio. General info, not legal advice.

Facilities managers: time the walk from your floor to the nearest food and back.

Texas has no state break law for adults, so your break policy sets the clock. If a 15-minute break is half gone before anyone eats, people come back late or skip it.

Our new guide covers what federal law requires, and how DFW sites make short breaks count.

https://texasvending.com/blog/texas-break-laws-employers/

Texas has no state law requiring meal or rest breaks for adult employees. That surprises a lot of facilities and HR teams.

Federal law still sets three rules for the breaks you do give:

1. Rest breaks of about 20 minutes or less are paid time (FLSA).
2. Meal periods can be unpaid only if the employee is completely relieved from duty. Watching a dock door while eating is work.
3. Under the PUMP Act, nursing employees get reasonable break time and a private space that is not a bathroom.

We wrote a plain-English guide with sources from the U.S. Department of Labor and a 6-point checklist for DFW sites:
https://texasvending.com/blog/texas-break-laws-employers/

General information, not legal advice.

Free vending is easy to find. Fair terms are not.

Before you sign with any vending company, ask:

• How long is the term, and does it auto-renew?
• Is it exclusive?
• Are there any fees, minimums, or removal charges?
• How fast do you fix a broken machine?
• Who removes the equipment at the end?

Get every answer in writing.

All 10 questions are in our new checklist. Link in bio.
